Westbury Violence

By: Tebadi Mmotla | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
It is a gangster paradise, Westbury a community filled with drugs, guns, and gangs.

Unique Selling Point:
For many years, Westbury has been engulfed with violence. There are constant shootings, with innocent community members being caught in the crossfire.

But Westbury’s gang violence is not a new phenomenon, it has been going on for decades. It dates back to the late 1960s, and early 1970s. The gangs: Fast guns, Varados, and Vultures were formed during this time. At that time these gangs were joined by individuals who were interested in soccer and Boxing. But soon that changed when drugs were introduced in the community.

Selling drugs became a lucrative business. The gangs moved to fighting and killing each other over territories to sell drugs.

After many years of back and forth between the three gangs, in 1999 they decided to call a truce. They met at Cecile Payne stadium and agreed on a peace deal. They handed over their guns, and burned flags associated with their gangs.

Some of the gang members went to church and became pastors, but others went back to their old ways and revived the gangs. Since then Westbury has been prone to violence.

In late February and March this year violence erupted in the community when an alleged leader of one of the gangs was shot dead.

Currently there is a heavy police presence in the area.


This story will look at the current targets of these gangs, pastors who were once gangsters. They are targeted under the notion of revenge, as people who once killed and went to jail, and therefore they need to pay for what they did. One of the pastors' who is targeted is Pastor Eugene Wheats. He is a former gangster, who was saved after the 1999 peace agreement. Last year when he was performing a graveside service, gangsters drove through and started shooting. He jumped into the grave hole.

When these kinds of drive through shootings happen, it is innocent community members who are caught in the crossfire. The story will also feature a mother who lost her child because of the violence.

The current gangs use young people to carry out the crimes. This includes the selling of drugs, hijackings, and killing the targets. As a result, the drugs and weapons end up at schools. Acting principal Westbury high School, who was also threatened with a gun by one of his students, will explain what the school is doing to fight violence.

Young people in Westbury are exposed to drugs and violence, where do they go to get away from the chaos.

Westbury Youth Center provides skills development to young people in the community. It is run by Brigit Munnik. She works with young people who are in school, those who left the gangs, and those who are unemployed and are recruited by the gangs. She replaces guns and drugs with skills development programs.


Summary:
Summary
This story will look at:

How community setup in Westbury makes it a gangsters’ paradise.
Introduction to drugs changed how gangsters operate.
A fight between gangsters, Now pastors who are former gangsters are being targeted
Community violence bleeds into schools
Centers accommodating young people.


PART ONE

The segment starts with clips of heavy police presence, and police arresting people.

Followed by a line explaining that Westbury is a community enveloped in violence, drugs, and gangsterism.

Clip of gunshots

Number of people get caught in the crossfire.

Gang rivals battle over streets and territories, leaving the community in fear.

But Westbury wasn't like that. Some say it all changed when drugs were introduced in the community.

PART TWO

Move to Church.

Pastor Eugine comes in and explains what Westbury used to look like as a young boy playing soccer.

Pictures of him as a young soccer player.
He explains how the gangs operated in the late 1960s and early 1970. Him being part of one of the gangs.

PART THREE

Move to Reverend Peter Faver. He will explain how the 1999 peace treaty was short lived.

He will speak on how the operations of the gangs changed. He will talk about how gangs are the core in the business of selling drugs, and how young people are recruited by these gangs, which is different from what they did back then.

He then talks about how they are targeted as former gangsters, and why he believes they are a target. He explains about how he was shot at the gym by a 16-year-old.

PART FOUR

Back to pastor Eugine. Just like Reverend Peter, he will explain how he was target while at a cemetery during a funeral

Highlights

Pastor Eugine:
shots of him in the church.
We took a walk with him to the graveyard. This is a place where he survived a drive through shooting, but also where he buries these young people. Also why people are afraid to go to funerals.

Reverent Peter:
Shoots of him at Kofifi Radio station.
Him working with youngsters who are former drug users.


PART FIVE

Three months ago one of the alleged gang leaders was gunned down. Since then there has been a heavy police presence in the area.

Here SAPS explains the strategy in place to deal with the violence. SAPS will also address the allegations of corrupt police officers who work with these gangsters, where in some instances some police officers were arrested.


PART SIX

A clip of students at Westbury High School

We explain that the violence in the community bleeds into schools, and Westbury High School is not an expansion.

Acting Principal Mr Dickson explains how some students bring weapons to school. Also how one student tried to shoot him in his office.

PART SEVEN

Clips showing what Westbury looks like. People standing in corners, taxi’s hooting, street vendors.

We ask where do young people in Westbury go, to get away from the chaos.

We introduce Westbury Youth Centre, managed by Brigit Munnik.

Brigit will talk about the plenty of resources available for young people in the community. How the center replaces drugs and guns, with skills development.


Highlights:

Brigit: Shots of different activities available at the center, that’s dancing, drama, singing, computer skills.
We walk with Brigit as she talks to young people who are not in school, and sitting by the corners.

Overall:
Painting Westbury.
Environmental noise.
Hero shots

Where homes and schools are no longer safe…


UPSOIND ISMAIL: He shot two times and then the third time the firearm jammed...
V/O


Children raised on a battlefield, their heroes – ruthless criminals…


UPSOUND Reverend Peter CLIP 0087 01:39 to 01:57: If I have to ask any of the kids, What would you like to be? I believe 99% will say drug lord because it's an easy life, lucrative life.

V/O:


We visit a community under siege … and find ordinary people holding the line against lawlessness...

VISUALS: P1024292.MOV: P1024293.MOV : Walking OR Driving into Westbury, woman hanging clothes, houses, life in westbury
UPSOUND FROM SHOW: REVEREND PETER FAVER

V/O:

CONTINUE TO HEAR AUDIO FROM THE STATION… VERY LOW IN THE BACKGROUND
V\O:
In a small studio at Westbury’s community Kofifi Radio, Reverend Peter Faver is preparing for his regular slot.

He’s lived in this troubled suburb his entire life.


UPSOUND: 00:43 – FAVER: WESTBURY has always been known for gangsterism, and drugs.

V/O:


Westbury rose from the forced removals of coloured people under Apartheid’s Group Areas Act in the 1960’s. Then, desperately poor, the area’s council flats became fertile breeding ground for drugs… and the gangs that trade them.


UPSOUND: AFTER 00:43 – FAVER: People are lured into selling drugs… with high unemployment rate in our community, the people that these kids are looking up to, they wear these big chains, bracelets, drive the most expensive cars...

V/O:


Now a man of the cloth, the Reverend understands all too well the temptations of this world.

Before finding religion, he led a much darker existence.


UPSOUND Reverend Peter: 02:08 to 08:13: I was the leader of the so-called Fast Guns. A very very notorious gang.

V/O:


Named after an old Hollywood action movie, the Fast Guns, are among four gangs that have terrorised Westbury for decades. Running gun battles with their arch enemies, the Varados, the Vultures and the Shed-No-Tears, are daily reminders of an endless struggle for control of the area’s drugs trade.
{PAUSE FOR THREE BEATS}


PRESENTER LINK:
Gang rivalries in Westbury have gotten so bad THAT Not even the dead are spared.
Last year mourners had to jump into empty graves when a shooting broke out at a funeral.
{PAUSE FOR THREE BEATS}
UPSOUND
Pastor Eugene: Young people are in deep trouble, because why? They refuse to follow the light.

V/O:

PASTOR Eugene Wheats heads another of Westbury’s churches and, with his colleagues, is involved in a tense stand-off with the gangs.


UPSOUND PASTOR EUGENE WHEATS 2:29 In the past we used to know who the gangsters is, today we don’t know, cause they are younger and you don’t know who to look out for.

V/O:

Despite his defiance, Wheats is heartbroken by the impact of the war being fought on these streets; on the community he loves and youngsters doing the fighting.


UPSOUND PASTOR EUGENE WHEATS 2:29 – Every community has different names for their gangs, but still it’s coloured people and our people are hurt. Losing a life, whether we say you’re a Varado or Fast Gun, or whatever, it hurts.

V/O:


Few households here have been spared the darkness and violence of the drugs trade. Many of the suburb’s young people join the gangs for a sense of belonging and to escape the ravages of poverty.


UPSOUND Reverend Peter 18:12 to 18:35: I lost my mom when I was eight years, Christmas day, my grannie boxing day... I had to fend for myself. At the age of nine, I was already selling newspapers.
Reverend Peter 18:38 to 18:42: … that lifestyle made us hardened, you understand?

Erin: to survive

Reverend Peter 18: 44 to 18:57: Yah to survive,

V/O:


Alarmingly, decades later, little has changed in Westbury. In fact, things may even be worse.
Change of gear hear … one or two beats … aerials visuals of Westbury to take to Aunty Brenda…


UPSOUND: 00:20 Brenda – Gavin is my son. He was gunned down on the 10th January 2021.

V/O:


Gavin Elias was 34-years old. On that Sunday evening, he was meters from home after returning from the shops with his son, Nathan.

His mother, Brenda, recalls what happened next.


UPSOUND BRENDA :
He saw people in our street with a broken down car and he helped them and while pushing the car, two guys approached him. All of a sudden, they just heard gunshots and we were in the house because it wasn’t far. And immediately I knew something is wrong.

V/O:


As Brenda and her husband rushed outside, she came face to face with her son’s killers.


UPSOUND BRENDA CLIP 0071 03:41 to 03:47: We saw the guys running that way with the guns. They, they don't hide the guns. They don’t hide it.


UPSOUND Erin: What were your last moments like with your son?


BRENDA CLIP 0071 16:55 to 17:06: I didn’t talk to him. Gavin was gone when I came there. He was already gone.


ERIN: Did you hold him?


BRENDA CLIP 0071: 17: 09 to 17:27 : I just prayed for him. There was nothing more I could do.

V/O:


In the last three years, 27 people have been killed in Westbury… all of them, gang related.

A level of violence Brenda finds impossible to escape.


In 2018, Gavin’s younger brother, Daren, was shot four times inside his yard.


UPSOUND BRENDA 5:13 – the shooting in my area, I saw the first time when my first son was shot in my yard. He came from work, he was a construction worker and he got shot and I could hear he’s calling my name.


VO: Daren survived, but his injuries were catastrophic, leaving him severely disabled and in need of constant care.


PRESENTER LINK
Children in Westbury often come from poverty-stricken homes -- survival depends on street smarts. Often that means turning to violence, gangsterism and drugs in order just to make it through.


UPSOUND 6:45 ISMAEL - Most of our cases is fighting, drugs, drug peddling, users of drugs, learner’s that’s high and we have to send them back home, because they are a danger to themselves.


VO: Westbury’s schools were once a rare safe haven from the gang violence, but learners now openly carry drugs and weapons.

Ismail Shahabodien, a former police officer, is chairman of one of the suburb’s high school governing bodies.


He says ensuring discipline in schools is difficult, if not impossible.





UPSOUND ISHMAEL 10:00 - You find a lot of times that in the households, there is no parents, there is grandparents and these learners will even go as far as to rob or even hit their own grandparents. You can actually see the physical marks on the grandparents and all the parent will say is that he or she don’t want to listen.


VO: But all is not lost in Westbury.


Despite its astonishingly high rate of fatherlessness, mothers continue fighting the good fight.


Bridget Munnik is determined to clean up her community. She’s created a safe haven for Westbury’s youth.


UPSOUND ERIN 16:09: Aunty Bree can you tell us why a center like this is important, especially in Westbury.


BRIDGET CLIP 0002.MXF: 00:37 to 00:48: Skills development is really good for the youth. After the three months you get your accredited certificate, you get into learnership.




VO: The Westbury Youth Center has been running for over 10 years now, aiming to replace guns and drugs with skills.


It’s clear many in this community, like Bridget, are simply not prepared to throw in the towel…




UPSOUND BRIDGET CLIP 0001.MXF: 11:44: 11:57 the only person that you can run to is God. A mother’s prayer is so, so crucial. So you need to keep, you need to be on your knees all the time…


BRIDGET CLIP 0001.MXF:12:17: But God, God always answers prayers.


VO: … it’s a prayer that Brenda also holds onto.


UPSOUND BRENDA 19:20:
He was my only child, my only child, I have six children, that call me Mummy. The others called me B. Now I will never hear him call me that again, but I’ve made peace with it. I’ve made peace.


PROMOS
PROMO 1 21”
VO: Westbury in Johannesburg... a continuous cycle of gangster turf wars, guns and drugs ...

UPS: Brenda: If you are just in the wrong territory and you are a young man, you're gonna die. You're gonna die.

VO: Here mothers are left with empty homes... and shattered hearts...

PROMO 2 21”
UPS: That side it’s Varados, there’s Fast Guns there...

VO: It’s a gangster’s paradise

UPS: Pastor Eugene: In the past we used to know who the gangster is, today we don’t, cause they are younger and you don’t know who to look out for.

VO: With constant senseless killings, Westbury in Johannesburg bears the scars of continued gangsterism.
PROMO 3 21”
Johannesburg’s western neighbourhood... , a community enveloped in drugs, guns and widespread shootings.

UPS: Pastor Eugene: Every third week we bury someone, your heart becomes sore.

VO: Can this cycle of criminality and violence ever come to an end?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): It is a gangster paradise, Westbury a community filled with drugs, guns, and gangs.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: For many years, Westbury has been engulfed with violence. There are constant shootings, with innocent community members being caught in the crossfire. But Westbury’s gang violence is not a new phenomenon, it has been going on for decades. It dates back to the late 1960s, and early 1970s. The gangs: Fast guns, Varados, and Vultures were formed during this time. At that time these gangs were joined by individuals who were interested in soccer and Boxing. But soon that changed when drugs were introduced in the community. Selling drugs became a lucrative business. The gangs moved to fighting and killing each other over territories to sell drugs. After many years of back and forth between the three gangs, in 1999 they decided to call a truce. They met at Cecile Payne stadium and agreed on a peace deal. They handed over their guns, and burned flags associated with their gangs. Some of the gang members went to church and became pastors, but others went back to their old ways and revived the gangs. Since then Westbury has been prone to violence. In late February and March this year violence erupted in the community when an alleged leader of one of the gangs was shot dead. Currently there is a heavy police presence in the area. This story will look at the current targets of these gangs, pastors who were once gangsters. They are targeted under the notion of revenge, as people who once killed and went to jail, and therefore they need to pay for what they did. One of the pastors' who is targeted is Pastor Eugene Wheats. He is a former gangster, who was saved after the 1999 peace agreement. Last year when he was performing a graveside service, gangsters drove through and started shooting. He jumped into the grave hole. When these kinds of drive through shootings happen, it is innocent community members who are caught in the crossfire. The story will also feature a mother who lost her child because of the violence. The current gangs use young people to carry out the crimes. This includes the selling of drugs, hijackings, and killing the targets. As a result, the drugs and weapons end up at schools. Acting principal Westbury high School, who was also threatened with a gun by one of his students, will explain what the school is doing to fight violence. Young people in Westbury are exposed to drugs and violence, where do they go to get away from the chaos. Westbury Youth Center provides skills development to young people in the community. It is run by Brigit Munnik. She works with young people who are in school, those who left the gangs, and those who are unemployed and are recruited by the gangs. She replaces guns and drugs with skills development programs.
metadata.Summary: Summary This story will look at: How community setup in Westbury makes it a gangsters’ paradise. Introduction to drugs changed how gangsters operate. A fight between gangsters, Now pastors who are former gangsters are being targeted Community violence bleeds into schools Centers accommodating young people. PART ONE The segment starts with clips of heavy police presence, and police arresting people. Followed by a line explaining that Westbury is a community enveloped in violence, drugs, and gangsterism. Clip of gunshots Number of people get caught in the crossfire. Gang rivals battle over streets and territories, leaving the community in fear. But Westbury wasn't like that. Some say it all changed when drugs were introduced in the community. PART TWO Move to Church. Pastor Eugine comes in and explains what Westbury used to look like as a young boy playing soccer. Pictures of him as a young soccer player. He explains how the gangs operated in the late 1960s and early 1970. Him being part of one of the gangs. PART THREE Move to Reverend Peter Faver. He will explain how the 1999 peace treaty was short lived. He will speak on how the operations of the gangs changed. He will talk about how gangs are the core in the business of selling drugs, and how young people are recruited by these gangs, which is different from what they did back then. He then talks about how they are targeted as former gangsters, and why he believes they are a target. He explains about how he was shot at the gym by a 16-year-old. PART FOUR Back to pastor Eugine. Just like Reverend Peter, he will explain how he was target while at a cemetery during a funeral Highlights Pastor Eugine: shots of him in the church. We took a walk with him to the graveyard. This is a place where he survived a drive through shooting, but also where he buries these young people. Also why people are afraid to go to funerals. Reverent Peter: Shoots of him at Kofifi Radio station. Him working with youngsters who are former drug users. PART FIVE Three months ago one of the alleged gang leaders was gunned down. Since then there has been a heavy police presence in the area. Here SAPS explains the strategy in place to deal with the violence. SAPS will also address the allegations of corrupt police officers who work with these gangsters, where in some instances some police officers were arrested. PART SIX A clip of students at Westbury High School We explain that the violence in the community bleeds into schools, and Westbury High School is not an expansion. Acting Principal Mr Dickson explains how some students bring weapons to school. Also how one student tried to shoot him in his office. PART SEVEN Clips showing what Westbury looks like. People standing in corners, taxi’s hooting, street vendors. We ask where do young people in Westbury go, to get away from the chaos. We introduce Westbury Youth Centre, managed by Brigit Munnik. Brigit will talk about the plenty of resources available for young people in the community. How the center replaces drugs and guns, with skills development. Highlights: Brigit: Shots of different activities available at the center, that’s dancing, drama, singing, computer skills. We walk with Brigit as she talks to young people who are not in school, and sitting by the corners. Overall: Painting Westbury. Environmental noise. Hero shots
